newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Australian markets wager on rate cut.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Australian markets wager on rate cut.

text.p: The final bets are almost in place, the form has been read and the odds have shortened, but unlike Australia's Melbourne Cup, financial markets are wagering on a one horse race -- a rate cut on Wednesday.

The markets have been more or less pricing in a 50 basis points reduction in official interest rates since the beginning of October, and economists believe the flow of economic data has been sufficiently weak to push the Reserve Bank's hand.
A survey of economists taken on Friday gave a better than even chance of an easing in November.

In Reuters' latest Australian Interest Rate Poll, economists were asked two questions; the probability of a cut in interest rates before the end of November in percentage terms, and before the end of the year.
The survey of 33 economists gave a median 65 percent probability of a rate cut in November following Tuesday's Reserve Bank of Australia monthly board meeting.

"I'm pretty much convinced that they are going to cut, but it is the wording that is going to be of interest in the statement along side it," said UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts, who gave a 90 percent chance of a November cut.
If the central bank leaves official interest rates on hold at 7.0 percent this month, economists gave a median 80 percent chance of an easing before the end of the year.

Economists were asked the same two questions on October 25 after quarterly inflation and wages data both proved benign, and well within the RBA's comfort zones. The median expectation then was 60 percent for a November cut, and 75 percent for December.

While the inflation and wages data are seen as the key elements leading to an interest rate reduction, in the past week the market has also seen unexpectedly sharp falls in both retail trade and building approvals data for September.

"Adding the weak retail sales report for September to the low September quarter inflation and wages reports, the weakness in capital goods imports, and the signs of a U.S. economic slowdown gives the Reserve Bank plenty of excuses to ease policy," said Andrew Pease at Nomura Research Australia.
These factors also combine with a flat labour market, weak business trading conditions and a fall in consumer confidence and point to an economy in need of a policy stimulus.
However, the big question mark is where policy goes from here if the RBA does cut rates tomorrow.
Before the market starts pricing in any further loosening in policy down the track, economists feel the RBA will want to see the extent of growth in enterprise bargaining agreements.

"I would be very surprised if there is not a paragragh or two just trying to point out that there is a sting in the tail to this rate cut, and that the Reserve bank stands ready to raise rates very promptly if we don't get moderation in enterprise deals," said UBS's Roberts.

The RBA expressed concern over wages growth through enterprise bargain agreements in its quarterly Bulletin three weeks ago, the only event that has soured policy easing expectations in the past month.
The latest report on these are expected sometime later this month.
The RBA last eased policy on July 31 by 50 basis points from 7.50 percent, a move that largely surprised the market.

But this time the markets are fully prepared with bond yields at their lowest levels since March 1994, the stock market around record highs, and the Australian dollar capped beneath 80 U.S. cents on the prospect of losing its yield advantage.
